Chapter 4 · Solving the PDE on a grid or a mesh: finite differences and finite elements

© 2026 Chantal Tax. All rights reserved. Shared for viewing only; not licensed for reuse or redistribution. Course: simulating the diffusion MRI signal. Chapters 2 and 3 needed a pore whose eigenmodes or closed forms are known. This chapter solves the Bloch–Torrey equation for any shape, by cutting space into pieces. What you'll take away
  1. The problem every simulator solves: tissue as compartments, each with its own diffusivity, relaxation time and spin density, joined by permeable interfaces.
  2. The method of lines: cut space into pieces and the Bloch–Torrey PDE becomes a large ODE system, with the same structure as the matrix method of Chapter 2.
  3. Finite differences as a flux balance between neighbouring cells: walls, membranes and relaxing walls are all rules for the flux through a face.
  4. Time stepping: explicit Euler, implicit Euler and Crank–Nicolson, their error orders, and the stability limit ||(\delta t\le h^2/(2dD)||).
  5. The matrix form used by GPU codes such as MATI: jump probabilities between voxels, an exact phase-and-relaxation factor, and the stability limit read as "no voxel gives away more than it holds".
  6. Periodic media simulated on a single cell, with a phase-shifted boundary condition.
  7. Finite elements from the weak form: why impermeable walls need no code, how a membrane enters, and the mass, stiffness, relaxation, gradient and interface matrices that SpinDoctor solves.
  8. Curved walls: a staircase grid against a mesh that follows the wall, and how fast each converges.
  9. How to choose ||(h||) and ||(\delta t||), and how to check any solver against Chapters 2 and 3.
Every exercise has hints and a worked answer, folded away. Try the exercise first, then open the hint, then the answer.

Units: lengths in µm, times in ms, gradients in mT/m, ||(\gamma = 2.6752\times10^{-4}||) rad/(ms·mT/m·µm). ||(D = 2||) µm²/ms throughout. Running example: a slab of width ||(L = 8||) µm, PGSE with ||(\delta = 10||) ms, ||(\Delta = 20||) ms and ||(G = 300||) mT/m. Its exact echo, from the MCF of Chapter 2, is ||(E = 0.171071||). Every solver in this chapter is tested against that number.

What you need from Chapters 1–3

Idea Formula
Bloch–Torrey ||(\partial M/\partial t = \nabla\cdot(D\nabla M) - i\gamma\,g(t)\,x\,M||), ||(\ M(\mathbf r, 0) = 1||), ||(\ E = \frac1V\int M(\mathbf r, T)\,d\mathbf r||)

Length scales ||(\ell_D = \sqrt{Dt}||), ||(\ \ell_g = (D/\gamma g)^{1/3}||), phase wavelength ||(2\pi/q||)
Tortuosity (Ch 3) membranes with spacing ||(L||): ||(1/D_\infty = 1/D + 1/(\kappa L)||)

  • Integration by parts in 1D: ||(\int_a^b wu'\,dx = [wu]_a^b - \int_a^b w'u\,dx||). In 3D, Green's first identity: ||(\int_\Omega w\,\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u) = \oint_{\partial\Omega} wD\,\partial_nu\,dS - \int_\Omega D\nabla w\cdot\nabla u||).

4.0 · From tissue to a matrix ODE

The problem: compartments joined by membranes

Chapters 1–3 solved the Bloch–Torrey equation in one pore at a time: a slab, a cylinder, a sphere. Tissue is a collection of such spaces: the inside of each cell, the space between the cells, perhaps organelles or myelin. Each has its own diffusivity and relaxation, and they are connected through membranes. Before choosing a numerical method, it is worth writing this problem down once in general, because every simulator in this chapter (and the Monte Carlo of Chapter 5) solves exactly this.
Symbol Meaning
||(\Omega = \bigcup_n\Omega_n||) the simulated piece of tissue, split into compartments ||(\Omega_n||)
||(\Gamma_{nm} = \partial\Omega_n\cap\partial\Omega_m||) the interface (membrane) between compartments ||(n||) and ||(m||)
||(\Gamma_n = \partial\Omega_n\cap\partial\Omega||) the part of ||(\Omega_n||) that lies on the outer boundary (may be empty)
||(D_n||), ||(T_{2,n}||), ||(\rho_n||) diffusivity, transverse relaxation time and spin density in ||(\Omega_n||)
||(\kappa_{nm} = \kappa_{mn}||) permeability of the interface ||(\Gamma_{nm}||)
||(\boldsymbol\nu_n||) unit normal on ||(\partial\Omega_n||), pointing out of ||(\Omega_n||)
||(f(t)\,\mathbf g||) the gradient: a fixed vector ||(\mathbf g||) times a time profile ||(f(t)||) (||(+1||) and ||(-1||) during the two PGSE lobes, 0 in between)
In each compartment the magnetization ||(M_n(\mathbf r, t)||) follows the Bloch–Torrey equation, now with relaxation: ||[\frac{\partial M_n}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot(D_n\nabla M_n) - \frac{M_n}{T_{2,n}} - i\gamma f(t)\,(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r)\,M_n,\qquad \mathbf r\in\Omega_n,\qquad M_n(\mathbf r, 0) = \rho_n .||]Three conditions close the problem:
Where Condition Meaning
outer boundary ||(\Gamma_n||) ||(D_n\,\partial_{\nu}M_n = 0||) no spins leave the simulated block
interface ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) ||(D_n\,\partial_{\nu_n}M_n = -D_m\,\partial_{\nu_m}M_m||) what leaves one side enters the other
interface ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) ||(D_n\,\partial_{\nu_n}M_n = \kappa_{nm}\big(c_{nm}M_m - c_{mn}M_n\big)||) the flux through the membrane is driven by the jump across it
The signal is the total magnetization at the echo time, ||(S = \int_\Omega M(\mathbf r, T_E)\,d\mathbf r||), and ||(E = S/\int_\Omega\rho||). → The equilibrium factors ||(c_{nm} = 2\rho_n/(\rho_n + \rho_m)||) matter only when two compartments hold different spin densities. They make sure that the equilibrium state, ||(M_n = \rho_n||) everywhere, drives no flux through any membrane (Exercise 6). For equal densities ||(c_{nm} = 1||), and the condition is the familiar ||(\kappa\times||) jump of Chapters 1 and 3. → Relaxation is the easy part. With one ||(T_2||) everywhere it simply multiplies the signal by ||(e^{-T_E/T_2}||) (Exercise 4). It matters when compartments relax differently: it then changes their weights in the signal, and with exchange it mixes with diffusion. → The outer boundary is artificial. A real tissue block continues beyond the simulated one. Reflecting walls are the simplest choice; one periodic cell (4a ⑥) avoids the artificial wall altogether. → The running example is the smallest case: one compartment (a slab), ||(\rho = 1||), no relaxation, a gradient along ||(x||). A membrane in the middle makes it two compartments when we need them.

The method of lines

Cut space into ||(n||) pieces and keep time continuous. Each piece carries one unknown, so the magnetization ||(M(x,t)||) becomes a vector ||(\mathbf M(t)||) and the Bloch–Torrey PDE becomes a system of ||(n||) linear ODEs: ||[\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}\,\frac{d\mathbf M}{dt} = -\big(D\,\mathbf K + i\gamma\,g(t)\,\mathbf X\big)\,\mathbf M .||]This is the method of lines: every point of space follows its own line in time, coupled to its neighbours. You met this form in Chapter 2, where the pieces were the eigenmodes. What changes from method to method is only the choice of pieces:
Modes (Chapter 2) Grid (finite differences) Hat functions (finite elements)
Unknowns coefficients ||(c_n||) of the eigenmodes one value ||(M_i||) per cell one value ||(M_i||) per node
||(M(x)||) rebuilt as ||(\sum_nc_nu_n(x)||): smooth, global piecewise constant piecewise linear
Diffusion matrix ||(\mathbf K||) ||(\Lambda||), diagonal neighbours only neighbours only
Gradient matrix ||(\mathbf X||) ||(\mathbf B||), dense ||(\mathrm{diag}(x_i)||) ||(\mathbf J||), neighbours only
Mass matrix ||(\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}||) identity identity ||(\int N_iN_j||), neighbours only
Geometry needs the modes of the shape any shape; walls become staircases any shape; walls lie on the mesh
→ In the mode basis diffusion is diagonal and the gradient couples every mode. On a grid the gradient is diagonal and diffusion couples neighbours. Same equation, opposite trade-off: modes are compact for simple shapes, grids and meshes work for any shape. → After this step, solving the PDE means two separate choices: how to cut space (sections 4a–4c) and how to step in time (section 4a ④). The figure shows the three ways of storing the same magnetization: a slab profile at the end of a short, strong gradient lobe, rebuilt from ||(n||) unknowns.

Grid: the 1D Laplacian has about ||(3\times10^3||), ||(\mathrm{diag}(x)||) has ||(10^3||). 4a · Finite differences

① The grid, and the Laplacian as a flux balance

Cut the pore into cells of width ||(h||), with one value ||(M_i||) at each cell centre ||(x_i||). Think of ||(M_i||) as the amount of magnetization in cell ||(i||), divided by its volume. Diffusion only moves magnetization between neighbouring cells, through the faces between them. ⇒ Fick's law at a face. The flux from cell ||(i||) to cell ||(i+1||) is ||(J_{i+1/2} = D\,(M_i - M_{i+1})/h||). ⇒ Balance of one cell. What enters through one face and leaves through the other changes the content of the cell: ||[h\,\frac{dM_i}{dt} = J_{i-1/2} - J_{i+1/2} = \frac Dh\big(M_{i-1} - 2M_i + M_{i+1}\big).||]⇒ Divide by ||(h||): the familiar three-point Laplacian, ||(D(M_{i-1} - 2M_i + M_{i+1})/h^2||). Taylor-expanding ||(M_{i\pm1}||) shows that it differs from ||(D\,M''(x_i)||) by ||(\frac{Dh^2}{12}M''''||): second order in ||(h||) (Exercise 2). → Writing the scheme as a flux balance (a finite-volume view) has two advantages. Magnetization is conserved exactly, because every flux leaves one cell and enters the next. And every kind of wall becomes a rule for the flux through one face.

② Walls, membranes and relaxing walls as face rules

Each face gets a conductance ||(c||), so that the flux is ||(c||) times the difference across it. In matrix form ||(d\mathbf M/dt = -\mathbf A\mathbf M||), a face between cells ||(i||) and ||(j||) adds ||(c/h||) to ||(A_{ii}||) and ||(A_{jj}||), and ||(-c/h||) to ||(A_{ij}||) and ||(A_{ji}||).
Face Flux through the face Conductance ||(c||)
bulk, between cells ||(i||) and ||(i+1||) ||(D(M_i - M_{i+1})/h||) ||(D/h||)
impermeable wall ||(0||) ||(0||) (the same as a "ghost cell" with ||(M_{\text{ghost}} = M_i||))
membrane with permeability ||(\kappa||) ||((M_i - M_{i+1})\big/\big(\frac h{2D} + \frac1\kappa + \frac h{2D}\big)||) ||(1/(h/D + 1/\kappa)||)
cells with different ||(D_i||), ||(D_{i+1}||) ||((M_i - M_{i+1})\big/\big(\frac h{2D_i} + \frac h{2D_{i+1}}\big)||) the harmonic mean of ||(D_i||), ||(D_{i+1}||), divided by ||(h||)
relaxing wall, relaxivity ||(\rho||) ||(M_i\big/\big(\frac h{2D} + \frac1\rho\big)||) out of the pore adds ||(c_w/h||) to ||(A_{ii}||) only, ||(c_w = 1/(h/2D + 1/\rho)||)
→ All the rules come from one idea: resistances in series. Between two cell centres the flux passes half a cell, perhaps a membrane, and another half cell. Their resistances ||(h/2D||), ||(1/\kappa||), ||(h/2D||) add. This is the same reasoning as the tortuosity formula of Chapter 3.

③ The gradient

The gradient term is local: each cell dephases at its own rate. It adds ||(i\gamma g(t)x_i||) to ||(A_{ii}||), a diagonal matrix. Relaxation is just as local: a cell in compartment ||(n||) gets an extra ||(1/T_{2,n}||) on the diagonal. Without relaxation, assembled: ||[\frac{d\mathbf M}{dt} = -\big(\mathbf A + i\gamma g(t)\,\mathrm{diag}(x_i)\big)\,\mathbf M,\qquad E = \frac1n\sum_iM_i\ \text{ at the echo}.||]Recipe ① Choose ||(h||) (see 4d) and place the cell centres. ② Give every face its conductance: bulk, wall, membrane or relaxing wall. ③ Assemble ||(\mathbf A||) and ||(\mathrm{diag}(x_i)||), start from ||(\mathbf M = 1||). ④ Step in time (next section) through the gradient waveform. ⑤ Average ||(\mathbf M||) over the cells at the echo.

④ Stepping in time

The ODE system ||(d\mathbf M/dt = -\mathbf A_g\mathbf M||), with ||(\mathbf A_g = \mathbf A + i\gamma g\,\mathrm{diag}(x)||), is stepped with one of three classic one-step methods:
Method One step Order Cost per step Stable for
explicit (forward) Euler ||(\mathbf M^+ = (\mathbf I - \delta t\,\mathbf A_g)\,\mathbf M||) 1 one sparse product ||(\delta t\le h^2/(2dD)||)
implicit (backward) Euler ||((\mathbf I + \delta t\,\mathbf A_g)\,\mathbf M^+ = \mathbf M||) 1 one sparse solve any ||(\delta t||)
Crank–Nicolson (trapezoid) ||((\mathbf I + \frac{\delta t}2\mathbf A_g)\,\mathbf M^+ = (\mathbf I - \frac{\delta t}2\mathbf A_g)\,\mathbf M||) 2 one sparse solve any ||(\delta t||)
(||(d||) is the number of space dimensions.) "Order ||(p||)" means that halving ||(\delta t||) divides the error at the echo by ||(2^p||). Crank–Nicolson is the average of the other two (Crank & Nicolson 1947). Why explicit Euler has a limit. Look at one Fourier pattern on the grid, ||(M_j = e^{ikjh}||). The three-point Laplacian maps it onto itself, multiplied by ||(-\mu||) with ||(\mu = \frac{4D}{h^2}\sin^2\frac{kh}2||). One explicit step therefore multiplies it by the amplification factor ||[G_{\text{EE}} = 1 - \delta t\,\mu = 1 - 4r\sin^2\tfrac{kh}2,\qquad r = \frac{D\,\delta t}{h^2}.||]The fastest pattern on the grid, ||(kh = \pi||) (neighbouring cells alternate), has ||(G = 1 - 4r||). For ||(r > 1/2||) that is below ||(-1||): this pattern flips sign and grows every step, and the solution blows up. Hence ||(\delta t\le h^2/(2D)||) in 1D, and ||(h^2/(2dD)||) in ||(d||) dimensions. This is the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy type of limit (Courant, Friedrichs & Lewy 1928). For the implicit methods: ||(G_{\text{IE}} = 1/(1 + 4r\sin^2\frac{kh}2)||) and ||(G_{\text{CN}} = (1 - 2r\sin^2\frac{kh}2)/(1 + 2r\sin^2\frac{kh}2)||). Both stay within ||([-1, 1]||) for every ||(r||). Crank–Nicolson's factor approaches ||(-1||) for large ||(r||): the fastest patterns are not damped but flip sign every step. That is harmless for a smooth start like ||(M = 1||), but it is why Crank–Nicolson can show small wiggles after a sudden change. data.text/markdown: What the right panel says. Explicit Euler needs 30 000 steps at ||(\delta t = 0.1\,h^2/2D||) for an error of ||(2\times10^{-5}||), and the error only halves when ||(\delta t||) halves. Crank–Nicolson takes steps 20 times larger than the explicit limit (||(\delta t = 0.2||) ms, 150 steps) and is still 5 times more accurate (||(4\times10^{-6}||)). Implicit Euler is stable at any step but, being first order, is the least accurate of the three at large steps. Each Crank–Nicolson step costs a sparse solve instead of a product, but in 1D that is cheap. → So why do GPU codes such as MATI step explicitly? In 3D a sparse solve is expensive and hard to parallelise, while an explicit step is the same small stencil for every voxel. Millions of voxels updated independently, many times, can beat fewer but sequential solves (section 4d). A trap for explicit Euler: the phase term. For the gradient alone, one explicit step multiplies ||(M_i||) by ||(1 - i\gamma gx_i\,\delta t||), whose modulus is ||(\sqrt{1 + (\gamma gx_i\delta t)^2} > 1||). Diffusion damps the fast patterns, but the uniform pattern is not damped, and its magnitude creeps up by about ||(\exp\big(\frac12(\gamma gx)^2\,\delta t\,T\big)||) over the sequence. A common cure is to apply the phase exactly, ||(M_i\to M_i\,e^{-i\gamma gx_i\delta t}||), and diffusion explicitly: an operator split, as in Chapter 2. That is the update of the next section.

With ||(s = \frac{\delta t}2\mu = 2r\sin^2\frac{kh}2\ge0||): ||(G = \frac{1-s}{1+s}\in(-1, 1]||). ✓ It tends to ||(-1||) for ||(s\to\infty||). (c) ⇒ At ||(r = 2||) explicit Euler amplifies the fast patterns (blow-up). Implicit Euler damps them, but too little. Crank–Nicolson keeps their size but flips their sign. All three are accurate for slow patterns (||(kh\ll1||)), where they follow the exact curve. → The start ||(M = 1||) and the smooth dephasing produce only slow patterns on a fine grid. The fast patterns carry almost nothing, so the implicit methods' errors there do not show in ||(E||). The explicit method is different: rounding errors seed the fast patterns, and instability then amplifies them from ||(10^{-16}||) to anything. (d) ⇒ ||(\gamma Gx = 2.6752\times10^{-4}\times300\times4 = 0.32||) /ms. ||(\delta t = 0.01/4 = 0.0025||) ms. data.text/markdown:
⑤ The matrix form used by GPU codes: jump probabilities

Write one explicit Euler step of the flux balance cell by cell, leaving the gradient out for a moment: ||[M_j^{+} = \big(1 - s_{j\to j-1} - s_{j\to j+1}\big)\,M_j + s_{j-1\to j}\,M_{j-1} + s_{j+1\to j}\,M_{j+1},\qquad s_{j\to k} = \frac{c_{jk}\,\delta t}{h} .||]⇒ Read it as bookkeeping. In one step a fraction ||(s_{j\to k}||) of the content of cell ||(j||) moves to cell ||(k||), and the rest stays. That is why ||(s||) is called a jump probability. In the bulk ||(s = D\,\delta t/h^2 = r||). ⇒ One number per face holds everything about the structure: the diffusivity, a membrane (||(c = 1/(h/D + 1/\kappa)||)), a wall (||(s = 0||)), a change of ||(D||). The structure enters only through these numbers, which are computed once, before the simulation starts. A Monte Carlo simulation instead meets the structure again in every step of every walker (Chapter 5). ⇒ The probability to stay must not be negative: ||(1 - s_{j\to j-1} - s_{j\to j+1}\ge0||), so ||(r\le\frac12||) in the bulk. This is the stability limit of ④ again, now with a physical reading: a cell cannot give away more than it holds. The matrix. Number the cells ||(1\dots n||) and collect the jump probabilities in a matrix ||(\mathbf S||): off the diagonal ||(S_{kj} = s_{j\to k}||), on the diagonal ||(S_{jj} = -\sum_ks_{j\to k}||). One diffusion step is ||(\mathbf M^+ = (\mathbf I + \mathbf S)\,\mathbf M||), and ||(\mathbf I + \mathbf S = \mathbf I - \delta t\,\mathbf A||) in the notation of ④. → Every column of ||(\mathbf S||) sums to zero: what leaves cell ||(j||) arrives in another cell. The total magnetization is conserved exactly, step after step. Relaxation and gradient as one factor. Over one step, relaxation and the gradient act on every cell separately, so they can be applied exactly: ||[\Phi_j = \exp\!\Big(-i\gamma f(t)\,(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r_j)\,\delta t - \frac{\delta t}{T_{2,j}}\Big),\qquad \mathbf M^{n+1} = \boldsymbol\Phi\odot(\mathbf I + \mathbf S)\,\mathbf M^n,||]where ||(\odot||) multiplies entry by entry. This is the matrix-based finite-difference (MFD) update of Xu, Does & Gore (2007): diffusion explicitly, everything local exactly. It removes the phase-term trap of ④. → In 3D, ||(\mathbf S||) couples each voxel to its six neighbours. MATI describes a substrate as a 3D matrix of labels (1 for the extracellular space, 2 for the intracellular space), turns the labels into jump probabilities once, and then repeats the same sparse product and entry-wise multiplication at every step: an ideal job for a GPU. The table runs this update on the running example. The time step is set through ||(r||), so ||(\delta t = rh^2/D||) shrinks with ||(h^2||).

It no longer commutes with the jumps: a spin's decay depends on how long it has stayed in each compartment. The signal is then not a product of a diffusion part and a relaxation part, and only a simulation (or a model of exchange, as in Chapter 3) can separate them.

data.text/markdown:
⑥ Periodic media: one cell with a phase-shifted boundary

Tissue is often modelled as a periodic array: the same cell repeated in every direction. Simulating a large block of cells is expensive, and its outer walls are artificial. Can one cell stand for the whole array? The diffusion problem is periodic, but the magnetization is not: the gradient makes ||(M||) wind faster and faster in space. The trick is to take out the winding. ⇒ Let ||(q(t) = \gamma\int_0^tg\,dt'||) and write ||(M = m\,e^{-iq(t)x}||). ⇒ Insert this into the Bloch–Torrey equation. The time derivative of the phase factor produces ||(-i\gamma gx\,m||), which cancels the gradient term exactly, and the Laplacian picks up the factor: ||(\partial_x(m\,e^{-iqx}) = e^{-iqx}(\partial_x - iq)\,m||). So ||[\frac{\partial m}{\partial t} = D\,(\partial_x - iq(t))^2\,m .||]⇒ This equation has no ||(x||) in it, only derivatives. For a periodic medium and a uniform start (||(m = 1||)), ||(m||) stays periodic. One cell with ordinary periodic boundaries is now enough. ⇒ On the grid, ||((\partial_x - iq)^2||) becomes the three-point stencil with phase factors on the neighbours: ||(\frac D{h^2}\big(e^{-iqh}m_{j+1} - 2m_j + e^{iqh}m_{j-1}\big)||). Each face carries its conductance times a phase factor that changes with ||(q(t)||). ⇒ At the echo ||(q(T) = 0||), so ||(E = \frac1V\int M = \frac1V\int m||). → The same trick without a change of variables. Keep ||(M||) itself on the grid, with the ordinary stencil and the gradient term of ③. Since ||(m||) is periodic and ||(M = m\,e^{-iqx}||), ||(M||) is periodic up to a phase: ||(M(x + L) = e^{-iq(t)L}\,M(x)||). So only the face that wraps from the last cell back to the first needs a phase factor, ||(e^{\mp iq(t)L}||). Across one period the gradient has added the phase ||(\gamma L\int_0^tg\,dt'||), and the boundary must know it. This is the revised periodic boundary condition of Xu, Does & Gore (2007), used in MATI. A plain periodic boundary, ||(M_{n+1} = M_1||), ignores the phase: it puts a false jump in ||(M||) at the wrap face, and an error in the signal. Both bookkeepings give the same signal at the echo, where ||(q = 0||). Finite elements use the same idea under the name pseudo-periodic conditions (Nguyen et al. 2014). Check: tortuosity. One cell of width ||(L = 8||) µm with a membrane on its face is an infinite stack of membranes. At long ||(\Delta||) and small ||(b||), the signal must decay as ||(e^{-bD_\infty}||), with ||(1/D_\infty = 1/D + 1/(\kappa L)||) from Chapter 3. The figure extracts ||(D_{\text{app}} = -\ln E/b||) from the single-cell simulation (narrow pulses: ||(\delta = 2||) ms, ||(G = 10||) mT/m).

4b · Finite elements

Finite differences ask the PDE to hold at the cell centres. Finite elements ask something weaker, which turns out to be more useful: that the PDE holds on average, against any weight function. The recipe has five steps, and each removes one difficulty.

① The weak form: weighted residuals

⇒ Write the PDE as residual ||(= 0||): ||(\ \partial_tM - \nabla\cdot(D\nabla M) + i\gamma g\,x\,M = 0||) in the domain ||(\Omega||). ⇒ Multiply by an arbitrary weight function ||(w(\mathbf r)||) and integrate over ||(\Omega||). If the result vanishes for every ||(w||), the residual itself must vanish: ||[\int_\Omega w\,\partial_tM\,d\mathbf r - \int_\Omega w\,\nabla\cdot(D\nabla M)\,d\mathbf r + i\gamma g\int_\Omega w\,x\,M\,d\mathbf r = 0 .||]⇒ Integrate the middle term by parts (Green's first identity). The second derivatives move half onto ||(w||), and a boundary term appears: ||[\int_\Omega w\,\partial_tM + \int_\Omega D\,\nabla w\cdot\nabla M + i\gamma g\int_\Omega w\,x\,M = \oint_{\partial\Omega}w\,D\,\partial_nM\,dS .||]This is the weak form. It only needs first derivatives of ||(M||), so ||(M||) may be built from pieces with kinks. ⇒ The boundary term holds the wall conditions. Look at what ||(D\,\partial_nM||) is on each kind of boundary:
Boundary Condition Boundary term ||(\oint wD\,\partial_nM||)
impermeable wall ||(D\,\partial_nM = 0||) ||(0||): nothing to code
relaxing wall ||(D\,\partial_nM = -\rho M||) ||(-\rho\oint w\,M\,dS||): a boundary "mass" term
membrane between ||(\Omega_1||) and ||(\Omega_2||) flux continuous ||(= \kappa\times||) jump ||(-\kappa\oint(M_1 - M_2)(w_1 - w_2)\,dS||), which couples the two sides (equal densities; Exercise 6 for the general case)
fixed value (||(M = M_0||)) — must be imposed on the unknowns directly
→ The first three are natural boundary conditions: they enter the weak form through the boundary integral, and are satisfied automatically by its solution. A fixed value is an essential condition, imposed by hand. Diffusion MRI needs only natural ones, which is why reflecting walls cost nothing in finite elements, while finite differences need a rule at every wall face.

② Galerkin: hat functions as unknowns and as weights

⇒ Cut ||(\Omega||) into elements (intervals in 1D, triangles in 2D, tetrahedra in 3D) with nodes at their corners. ⇒ Give each node ||(j||) a hat function ||(N_j||): 1 at node ||(j||), 0 at every other node (||(N_j(\mathbf r_i) = \delta_{ij}||)), linear on each element. Write ||(M(\mathbf r, t)\approx\sum_jM_j(t)\,N_j(\mathbf r)||): the unknowns are the nodal values. ⇒ Use the same hats as weights, ||(w = N_i||) for each ||(i||) (Galerkin's choice, 1915). Each weight gives one equation, so there are as many equations as unknowns. ⇒ In one element of length ||(h||) with local coordinate ||(\xi\in[-1, 1]||), ||(x = \frac{x_a + x_b}2 + \frac h2\xi||), the two hats are ||(N_1 = \frac12(1-\xi)||) and ||(N_2 = \frac12(1+\xi)||). Three nodes per element give quadratic shapes, ||(\frac12\xi(\xi-1)||), ||((1-\xi)(1+\xi)||) and ||(\frac12\xi(\xi+1)||).

③ Element matrices and assembly

⇒ Insert ||(M = \sum_jM_jN_j||) and ||(w = N_i||) into the weak form. Every integral becomes a sum over elements of small matrices: ||[\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}\frac{d\mathbf M}{dt} = -\big(\mathbf K + i\gamma g(t)\,\mathbf J\big)\mathbf M,\qquad \mathcal M_{ij} = \int N_iN_j,\quad K_{ij} = \int D\,\nabla N_i\cdot\nabla N_j,\quad J_{ij} = \int N_i\,x\,N_j .||]For a 1D element ||([x_a, x_b]||) of length ||(h||), all three integrals are exact: ||[\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}^e = \frac h6\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf K^e = \frac Dh\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf J^e = \frac h{12}\begin{pmatrix}3x_a + x_b & x_a + x_b\\ x_a + x_b & x_a + 3x_b\end{pmatrix}.||]⇒ Assembly. Each element adds its ||(2\times2||) matrix into the rows and columns of its two nodes. Neighbouring elements share a node, so their contributions overlap there. The result is a sparse matrix that couples each node only to its neighbours. → For linear triangles in 2D the same integrals have closed forms: ||(\mathbf K^e = D(\mathbf b\mathbf b^{\mathsf T} + \mathbf c\mathbf c^{\mathsf T})/(4A)||), with ||(b_i||), ||(c_i||) differences of the corner coordinates and ||(A||) the area; ||(\mathcal M^e_{ij} = \frac A{12}(1 + \delta_{ij})||); and ||(\int N_1^aN_2^bN_3^c\,dA = 2A\,\frac{a!\,b!\,c!}{(a+b+c+2)!}||) for ||(\mathbf J^e||). For curved or higher-order elements the integrals are mapped to a reference element (isoparametric mapping) and done by Gauss quadrature.

④ The full system: compartments, relaxation and membranes

With several compartments, each gets its own set of hat functions, living only on the elements of that compartment. A node on an interface ||(\Gamma_{nm}||) is therefore doubled: one copy belongs to ||(\Omega_n||), the other to ||(\Omega_m||), so that ||(M||) can jump across the membrane (⑥ shows it in 1D). Put all nodal values in one vector ||(\boldsymbol\xi||) and write ||(\varphi_k||) for the hat function of node ||(k||). The weak form of the problem of 4.0 then gives ||[\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}\,\frac{d\boldsymbol\xi}{dt} = -\big(\mathbf S + \mathbf R + \mathbf Q + i\gamma f(t)\,\mathbf J(\mathbf g)\big)\,\boldsymbol\xi,\qquad \xi_k(0) = \rho_n\ \text{ for every node } k \text{ of } \Omega_n .||]
Matrix Entries Comes from
||(\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}||), mass ||(\int\varphi_k\varphi_l||) the time derivative
||(\mathbf S||), stiffness ||(\int D_n\nabla\varphi_k\cdot\nabla\varphi_l||) diffusion
||(\mathbf R||), relaxation ||(\frac1{T_{2,n}}\int_{\Omega_n}\varphi_k\varphi_l||): each compartment's mass matrix divided by its ||(T_2||) relaxation
||(\mathbf J(\mathbf g)||), gradient ||(\int\varphi_k\,(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf r)\,\varphi_l||) the gradient
||(\mathbf Q||), interface ||(\kappa_{nm}\int_{\Gamma_{nm}}\varphi_k\varphi_l||), weighted by ||(c_{mn}||) or ||(-c_{nm}||) (Exercise 6) the membrane term of the weak form
→ In the 1D notation of ③, ||(\mathbf K = \mathbf S + \mathbf Q||), ||(f(t)\,\mathbf J(\mathbf g)||) is ||(g(t)\,\mathbf J||), and ||(\mathbf R = 0||). → All five matrices are sparse and are assembled once. SpinDoctor (Li et al. 2019) builds them on a tetrahedral mesh and hands the ODE system to an adaptive solver for stiff problems (MATLAB's ode23t, a trapezoidal rule with error control), which picks its own time steps. The signal is ||(S = \sum_kw_k\xi_k||) with ||(w_k = \int\varphi_k||).

⑤ Time stepping and the signal

Crank–Nicolson with the mass matrix: ||(\ (\boldsymbol{\mathcal M} + \frac{\delta t}2\mathbf A_g)\,\mathbf M^+ = (\boldsymbol{\mathcal M} - \frac{\delta t}2\mathbf A_g)\,\mathbf M||), with ||(\mathbf A_g = \mathbf K + i\gamma g\,\mathbf J||). The signal is the integral of ||(M||): ||(\ E = \frac1V\sum_iw_iM_i||) with ||(w_i = \int N_i||), the row sums of ||(\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}||). → Replacing ||(\boldsymbol{\mathcal M}||) by the diagonal matrix of row sums ("mass lumping") turns linear finite elements on a uniform 1D grid into the finite-difference scheme of 4a. The two methods are close relatives; they part ways in how they handle geometry.

⑥ Membranes, and the check against Chapter 1

Chapter 1 (Exercise 9) found the exchange mode of a slab ||([-a, a]||) with a membrane in the middle: its rate ||(Dk^2||) follows from ||(k\tan(ka) = 2\kappa/D||). data.text/markdown:
4c · Curved walls: a staircase or a fitted mesh

In 1D every wall sits on a face or a node, and finite differences and finite elements are equally good (4d shows it). The difference appears with curved walls. A Cartesian grid can only follow a circle as a staircase of cell faces. A triangle mesh puts its boundary nodes on the circle, so its boundary is a polygon whose corners lie on the wall. The test: the slowest non-uniform mode of a disk of radius ||(R||) (the cross-section of a cylinder), whose exact eigenvalue is ||(\lambda_1R^2 = 1.8412^2 = 3.3900||) (Chapter 1). It sets the slowest decay inside an axon, so every restricted-diffusion signal depends on it.

data.text/markdown: Reading the result. With about the same number of unknowns, the mesh is 4 to 16 times more accurate, and the gap grows with resolution. Its error falls as ||(h^2||), steadily. The grid's error falls only as ||(h||) on average, and erratically: the staircase changes shape in jumps as ||(h||) shrinks, and a slightly finer grid can even be worse (compare ||(R/h = 6||) and 8). → A grid misplaces the wall by up to half a cell, an ||(O(h)||) error in the shape, so first-order convergence is the best it can do near curved walls. Finite-difference codes reduce this with finer voxels near the walls or with "cut-cell" corrections. Finite elements avoid it by construction, at the price of generating the mesh.

• (a) Follow the staircase over one quarter of the circle: how far does it go horizontally in total, and how far vertically?
  • (b) The eigenvalue depends on the volume and on where the boundary is, not on how long it is. How far is the staircase from the circle?

(a) ⇒ Over a quarter circle the staircase moves ||(R||) horizontally and ||(R||) vertically in total, however small the steps: length ||(2R||) per quarter, ||(8R||) in all. The ratio to the true perimeter is ||(8R/2\pi R = 4/\pi = 1.27||). ⇒ The area converges to ||(\pi R^2||), so the voxelised disk has ||(S/V\to8/(\pi R)||) instead of ||(2/R||): 27% too large, at every resolution. (In 3D a voxelised sphere has a surface area 1.5 times too large, for the same reason.) (b) ⇒ The staircase is never further than about ||(h||) from the circle. The eigenvalue depends on the shape through the region it encloses, which converges to the disk as ||(h\to0||). The length of a curve is not a continuous function of the curve: a zig-zag can be arbitrarily close to a line and still be longer. (c) ⇒ At diffusion lengths comparable to the voxel size, spins can feel the steps, and quantities that depend on the wall area, such as the Mitra short-time slope, can inherit the wrong ||(S/V||). Check against the closed form of Chapter 3 for a shape with known ||(S/V||) (a cylinder or a sphere), and refine the voxels near the wall until the short-time slope is right. At diffusion lengths much larger than the steps, the walls are effectively smooth again.

data.text/markdown:
Both errors fall as ||(h^2||), four times per halving, and in 1D the two methods are equally accurate. The differences are elsewhere:
Finite differences (e.g. MATI) Finite elements (e.g. SpinDoctor)
Geometry voxel grid; curved walls become staircases triangles or tetrahedra that follow the walls
Input a segmented image, used directly a surface mesh, which must be filled with tetrahedra
Walls and membranes a rule for the flux through every wall face natural in the weak form; membranes by double nodes
Convergence near curved walls ||(O(h)||), erratic ||(O(h^2)||) for linear elements
Time stepping explicit: no solve, but ||(\delta t\le h^2/(2dD)||) implicit or adaptive: large steps, one sparse solve each
Cost driver voxels × steps, trivially parallel (GPU) meshing, then sparse factorisations; fewer unknowns per accuracy
Extras periodic cells with a phase-shifted boundary eigenmodes on the mesh for the matrix method (4b ⑦)
→ The equation is the same; the difference is how space and time are cut. A grid gives up geometric fidelity and takes tiny time steps, in exchange for an update so simple that a GPU can run millions of voxels at once. A mesh pays for meshing and linear solves, in exchange for walls exactly where they are and large time steps.

Choosing ||(h||) and ||(\delta t||)

① Space. ||(h||) must resolve the finest pattern in ||(M||): the smallest of the structure you care about, the gradient length ||(\ell_g = (D/\gamma g)^{1/3}||) and the phase wavelength ||(2\pi/q||), with at least a few cells per length, better 5–10. ② Time, explicit. ||(\delta t\le h^2/(2dD)||) for stability, and small enough to follow the waveform. ③ Time, implicit. ||(\delta t||) set by accuracy alone: Crank–Nicolson needs a few steps per change of the gradient, more for oscillating waveforms. ④ Check. Halve ||(h||), then ||(\delta t||), until ||(E||) changes by less than you can measure. ⑤ Validate. Before simulating tissue, reproduce a slab, a cylinder or a sphere: the exact MCF of Chapter 2, and the closed forms of Chapter 3 (form factor, motional narrowing, localisation). If two methods disagree on a slab, one of them has a bug.

(a) ⇒ ||(\gamma G = 2.6752\times10^{-4}\times300 = 0.0803||) rad/(ms·µm). ||(\ell_g = (2/0.0803)^{1/3} = 2.9||) µm. ||(q = \gamma G\delta = 0.80||) µm⁻¹, so ||(2\pi/q = 7.8||) µm. ||(\ell_g||) is smaller: ||(h\lesssim\ell_g/5\approx0.6||) µm, and finer if the structure (membranes, small cells) demands it. (b) ⇒ ||((20/0.2)^3 = 10^6||) voxels. ||(\delta t\le h^2/(6D) = 0.04/12 = 3.3||) µs, so ||(30/0.0033\approx9000||) steps. About ||(9\times10^9||) voxel updates: about one second at ||(10^{10}||) updates per second. Halving ||(h||) multiplies this by 32 (8 times more voxels, 4 times more steps). (c) ⇒ The cost of a sparse solve in 3D grows faster than linearly with the number of nodes and parallelises less well, while the explicit stencil is linear and embarrassingly parallel. A mesh wins when far fewer unknowns are needed (curved walls, local refinement), when large time steps are allowed (long sequences), or when the eigenmodes can be reused for many sequences (4b ⑥). A grid wins for very large segmented volumes on a GPU. Either way, check against Chapters 2 and 3 first.
